issues.issue: The dividend right is left wholly to "the conditions fixed and determined by the Board of Directors," so the promise that "you shall participate" has no ascertainable content. A court could be asked whether this creates any enforceable entitlement at all.

"09/01/2012 to 09/01/2013 at 12:01 A.M. standard time" does not say whether the terminal date is included, so a loss on 09/01/2013 is of uncertain coverage. The single time stamp is applied to both dates without distinguishing inception from expiry.

"Risks of direct physical loss or damage" is undefined and its boundary — whether cosmetic, functional or merely diminished-value harm counts as "direct physical loss or damage" — is the classic battleground of an all-risk grant. The phrase "unless excluded" also leaves the burden and reach of the exclusions to be worked out.

The grant turns on "an accident to an object," both defined terms whose exclusions (DEFINITIONS A. and Y.) carve out gradually developing conditions and structural parts, leaving the boundary of this grant contestable. Whether a given failure is an "accident" rather than wear is left to construction.

This paragraph says insurance is provided "at those locations ... shown on the Schedule of this form," but the Schedule (c028) shows no individual locations and instead refers to a Statement of Values on file. The two cannot both be given literal effect as to which locations are insured.

The convention that "words in bold faced type have special meanings" depends on typography that the issued document does not reliably carry, so which occurrences of terms like "covered location" or "occurrence" are defined uses is uncertain. A court could be asked whether an unbolded use takes the defined meaning.

This paragraph promises "coverage on a replacement cost basis" while VALUATIONS A. 2. (c128) withholds replacement cost until property is actually repaired or replaced and pays only actual cash value after two years. The two must be reconciled to know what the insured is entitled to.

The cap is per "any one (1) occurrence," but DEFINITIONS Z. (c235) aggregates all loss from "one cause or series of similar causes" irrespective of time or area, so the number of occurrences in a multi-storm or multi-building claim is left open. How this limit applies depends entirely on that definition.

"If no sublimit is shown, no coverage is provided" sits against EXTENSIONS OF COVERAGE B. 9. (c099), which states flatly that unscheduled locations are insured for the coverages marked with an "X". Which controls where the Declarations show "$No Coverage" is a question of construction.

"Coverage may be limited or excluded elsewhere in this policy or its endorsements" states a possibility rather than a rule, so it gives no guidance on which limitation governs. The word "may" leaves the provision without operative content.

The "lesser of" test refers to "the sublimit shown on any individual coverage form or endorsement" without saying which form applies when several show different sublimits. The comparison is therefore indeterminate on its own terms.

The box selects "See the Schedule of this form" while every dollar entry in the same item reads "$Not Applicable," and the descriptive captions are detached from the amounts. The item is internally inconsistent about whether any equipment breakdown limit is stated here.

The $10,000 flat deductible is stated but the same item also checks "See ADDITIONAL DEDUCTIBLES AND WAITING PERIODS, Form RM1115" (c314), which supplies different and percentage-based deductibles. Which deductible governs a given loss must be worked out between the two.

A waiting period of "Not Applicable hours" is not a number, leaving it unclear whether no waiting period applies or the coverage condition cannot be satisfied. The same blank is repeated in Form RM1115 (c325).

The "largest of the applicable deductibles" rule is expressly subject to Form RM1115, whose paragraph C. (c316) makes asterisked deductibles cumulative instead. Whether deductibles stack in a given loss depends on reconciling the two.

The Schedule names no locations and instead insures "All covered locations as per Statement of Values on file with us," while DEFINITIONS E. (c214) defines covered location(s) as those "shown on the Schedule of the DECLARATIONS" — a circle that leaves the insured locations to be established outside the policy. Which document fixes the covered locations is squarely contestable.

"Insurance does not apply at locations and/or coverages at locations unless a specific value is provided by you" makes coverage turn on an extrinsic Statement of Values whose content, date and required level of detail are nowhere specified. What counts as "a specific value" for a location or coverage is undefined.

The grant covers real property "at or within one-thousand (1,000) feet of a covered location," so its whole reach depends on the contested identification of covered locations under the Schedule (c028) and DEFINITIONS E. (c214). Property at an unlisted address may or may not fall within the grant.

Like the real property grant, this one is tied to "a covered location," whose identification depends on the Statement of Values reference in the Schedule (c028) rather than any list in the policy. The scope of the grant cannot be fixed without resolving that.

Items 3. and 4. here cap civil-authority and ingress/egress business income at twenty-one days with no dollar limit, but the RM1525 and RM1526 endorsements (c369, c371) delete and replace them with thirty days subject to a $1,000,000 limit. The printed form and the endorsements state different terms for the same coverage.

"Consideration must be given to" the listed factors states no weighting or method, so the resulting business income figure is not determinable from the text. "Probable experience after the loss" is inherently open-ended.
"Wholly or partially prevented from producing goods" sets no threshold of interference, so any degree of slowdown may or may not trigger coverage. The term "partially prevented" has no boundary.

The mitigation list is mislettered and its lead-in items are detached from their text, and it requires making up lost production "within a reasonable period of time not limited to the period of restoration" without any outer bound. The duty's extent is not ascertainable from the words.

The idle-period exclusion sweeps in any period when operations would cease "due to ... any reason other than a covered loss," language broad enough to swallow the business income grant in C. 1. Where the ordinary causes of an interruption overlap, the exclusion's reach is contestable.

The twenty-one-day civil authority extra expense period stated here is deleted and replaced by the RM1523 endorsement (c367), which sets thirty days and a $1,000,000 limit. The form as printed states a different term from the endorsement governing the same subject.

"Any loss or expense recoverable elsewhere in this policy" is excluded without saying whether "recoverable" means actually payable or merely arguably within another grant. That phrase can be read to defeat overlapping coverages entirely.

This paragraph pays to dry out electrical objects damaged by "the peril of flood" although GROUP A exclusion 3. (c103) excludes flood and the FLOOD COVERAGE endorsement provides flood cover only at scheduled locations. Whether dry-out costs are payable where flood is otherwise excluded requires reconciling the three.

The $100,000 accounts receivable limit stated here is increased to $1,000,000 by the STANDARD EXTENSIONS AMENDATORY endorsement (c327), so the figure in this text is not the operative one. A reader relying on this paragraph alone is misled as to the limit.

"All reasonable efforts, including legal action if necessary" sets no benchmark for how far the insured must pursue debtors before recovery is reduced. Whether suit was "necessary" is left to argument.

The averaging formula is "adjusted for normal fluctuations" and "any demonstrated variance," neither of which is defined or measurable from the policy. The computation cannot be performed from the text alone.

The reward is triggered by "fires of a suspicious nature," a phrase with no stated test, while payment also requires conviction or confession — two different standards in the same clause. What makes a fire "suspicious" is left undefined.

This "extension" is drafted in exclusionary form — paying "for loss or damage to, or any cost, claim or expense caused by or resulting directly or indirectly from" the listed computer events "regardless of any other cause" — so it is unclear whether it grants coverage or merely caps it. The concluding catch-all "any other electronic equipment, computerized equipment, or similar device" adds a general-versus-specific problem.

Payment is conditioned on "immediate written notice," a term with no fixed period and no stated consequence of delay short of forfeiture. Whether notice was "immediate" is a classic construction question.
The $250,000 debris removal sublimit stated here is increased to $1,000,000 by the STANDARD EXTENSIONS AMENDATORY endorsement (c330). The operative figure is not the one in this paragraph.

This $25,000 windblown-debris provision is deleted and replaced with a $50,000 version by the STANDARD EXTENSIONS AMENDATORY endorsement (c331). Both texts appear in the delivered policy stating different amounts.
"All reasonable effort, including legal action against your client" fixes no limit on the collection steps required before the insurer will pay. The duty's extent is left to argument.

The list of "all of the following conditions" is broken by page-break text and mislettered items, so the conditions cannot be read as a coherent enumerated set. Which conditions must coexist is obscured by the mechanical defect.

The sixty-day extended period stated here is amended to ninety days by the STANDARD EXTENSIONS AMENDATORY endorsement (c333), so the printed figure is superseded. Both figures appear in the delivered policy.

This paragraph disapplies "the exclusions and restrictions in this policy regarding loss of your market share," but the policy contains no market-share exclusion — only GROUP B exclusion 6. (c117) for "loss of market." What is being disapplied has to be inferred.
The promise to pay "charges you incur when the fire department is called" states no sublimit and no requirement that the charges be reasonable or legally owed. Its outer boundary is left open.

The breakage carve-out applies to listed fragile items "and similar fragile articles," a catch-all sitting against a closed list of specifics. What is "similar" is exactly the ejusdem generis question.

The fire-or-lightning fungus branch pays "up to the applicable limit of liability," without saying which of the policy's several limits or sublimits is "applicable." The sentence is also broken mid-phrase by the stray subparagraph marker.
Coverage is conditioned on "immediate written notice of the covered loss," a term with no defined period. Whether notice was timely under this condition is left to construction.

Coverage lasts only "if your responsibility continues until the purchaser accepts the installation," with neither "responsibility" nor "accepts" defined. The end of the coverage period is therefore uncertain.

This extension states no sublimit of its own while the closing sentence of the standard extensions (c084) assumes each carries one, leaving the amount payable for employees' property unfixed. Whether the blanket limit or some sublimit applies is open.

This grant pays to remove pollutants "subject to the applicable limit of liability" although GROUP A exclusion 5. (c105) excludes "Pollution" outright and without a stated carve-back. Which prevails for specified-peril pollution has to be construed.
The $25,000 annual aggregate stated here is raised to $50,000 by the STANDARD EXTENSIONS AMENDATORY endorsement (c339). The operative aggregate is not the one printed in this paragraph.
The $25,000 annual aggregate here is raised to $50,000 by the STANDARD EXTENSIONS AMENDATORY endorsement (c340), so the figure in this text is superseded. Both appear in the delivered policy.
The $25,000 professional fees sublimit is increased to $50,000 by the STANDARD EXTENSIONS AMENDATORY endorsement (c341). The printed amount is not the operative one.

Removal costs are payable only for property under "imminent threat by a peril insured against," a standard with no temporal or probabilistic content. Whether a threat was "imminent" is left entirely to argument.

The ninety-day temporary-location period stated here is deleted and replaced by the STANDARD EXTENSIONS AMENDATORY endorsement (c342) with "up to NA days," leaving no ascertainable period. The two texts cannot both be given effect.

This anti-stacking sentence says extension sublimits "do not increase and are not in addition to" other limits, while CONDITIONS O. No Reduction by Loss (c169) says payment of a covered loss does not reduce other applicable limits or sublimits. How the two interact where several sublimits touch one loss is unresolved.

Optional extensions "apply only if the applicable sublimit ... is shown" in the Declarations, yet B. 4., B. 5. and B. 9. (c092, c093, c099) state affirmatively that miscellaneous, new and unscheduled locations are insured. The condition and those grants pull against each other where the Declarations show "$No Coverage".

Coverage runs "sixty (60) days from the date you begin construction," but nothing defines when construction is "begun" — site work, permitting or first materials. The start of the sixty-day clock is left open.

Coverage applies only where a loss is unpayable "solely because of an error or unintentional omission" in describing where property is located or in including a location, and is then withdrawn "if coverage is found, in whole or in part, elsewhere in this policy." "Solely" and the "in whole or in part" cut-back can be read to cancel the grant in the very case it was written for.

The extension is aimed at omissions in the description of location, but the Declarations Schedule (c028) makes insurance depend on a value being "provided by you" in a Statement of Values held by the insurer. Whether a failure of that reporting is an insured "error or unintentional omission" is a question of how the two provisions stand together.

"Miscellaneous locations are insured" for the marked coverages, but DEFINITIONS T. (c229) defines a miscellaneous location purely by exclusion of covered, new and unscheduled locations, and DECLARATIONS E. (c016) says no coverage exists without a stated sublimit. The grant's scope is only intelligible when read against those two.

The period of new-location coverage is fixed by reference to "E. 4. h. of the DECLARATIONS," an item whose lettering and amounts are detached from their captions in the delivered form. The cross-reference cannot be resolved on the face of the policy.

This extension pays demolition, increased construction and building-law costs although GROUP A exclusion 6. (c106) excludes those very costs outright. Which governs a given ordinance-driven cost requires reconciling the exclusion with this grant.

This says unscheduled locations "are insured" for the marked coverages, while DECLARATIONS E. 1. (c016) and EXTENSIONS B. lead-in (c085) provide that no coverage exists unless a sublimit is shown, and the Declarations list shows "$No Coverage" for unscheduled locations. Whether property at an unlisted location is covered turns on which of these controls.

This excludes earth movement "whether sudden or gradual," while the EARTH MOVEMENT COVERAGE endorsement (c273) buys back only "sudden earth movement" at scheduled locations. Whether a particular movement is sudden, and so restored to coverage, depends on reading the two together.

Flood is excluded here, but the FLOOD COVERAGE endorsement (c284) restores it at scheduled locations and COVERAGES E. 3. (c042) pays dry-out costs for electrical objects damaged by flood. The interaction of the exclusion with those two grants must be construed.

Fungus is excluded except where loss "from a specified peril ensues," yet the Fungus Cleanup extension (c068, c069) pays cleanup costs where fungus results from a covered loss by fire, lightning or any other insured peril. The exclusion and the extension describe overlapping but differently bounded coverage.

The one-word exclusion "Pollution." carries no ensuing-loss carve-back, yet the Pollution Cleanup Expense extension (c077-c079) pays to remove pollutants in defined circumstances. Which provision governs cleanup costs after an insured peril must be settled between them.

This excludes demolition, building-law and increased construction costs absolutely, while EXTENSIONS B. 6. (c095) grants exactly those costs when a sublimit is shown. The exclusion and the optional extension cannot both be applied literally.

The carve-back for "acts of destruction ordered by government to prevent the spread of fire" overlaps GROUP B exclusion 14. (c125), which excludes acts or decisions of any governmental body subject to an ensuing-loss proviso. Which of the two governs a government-ordered destruction is not settled by either text.

This excludes utility interruption where "the failure occurs away from the covered location," while the INTERRUPTION OF SERVICES COVERAGE EXTENSION (c296) insures precisely off-premises service interruptions at scheduled locations. The exclusion's continuing reach after the endorsement has to be construed.

"Any virus, organism or like substance that is capable of inducing disease, illness, physical distress or death" is open-ended, and "like substance" is a catch-all following broad specifics. Whether ordinary bacteria, mold or contaminants fall in is left to construction.

The exclusion reaches "any other electronic equipment, computerized equipment, or similar device" and any "change in the functionality, availability, operation, use of, accessibility to" those items, wording broad enough to catch ordinary equipment damage. The catch-all against the enumerated computer items is a general-versus-specific problem.

The provision is printed with orphan numbering ("1. 2 3.") preceding the text, so it is not clear which exclusion this sentence is or what the other numbered items are. The mechanical defect obscures the enumeration of GROUP B.

"Theft by employees" sits against the carve-back in exclusion B. 4. that acts of destruction, including vandalism, by employees are not excluded. Which rule applies where an employee both destroys and takes property must be construed between the two.

Subparagraph c. is mutilated — "any of your associates, proprietors, partners, directors, trustees, officers, _ oo or representatives voluntarily relinquishes possession of covered property with or without your" — so the class of persons and the qualifying condition are missing. The exclusion's scope cannot be determined from its own words.

This excludes "loss of use" and "indirect or remote loss" without any ensuing-loss proviso, while COVERAGES C. and D. (c031, c037) insure loss of business income and extra expense, which are by nature indirect losses of use. Whether the exclusion cuts into those grants is a genuine conflict.

The exclusion covers "wear and tear, deterioration ... rust, corrosion" and "any quality in the covered property that causes it to damage or destroy itself," but pays where "a covered loss ensues," a sequence the clause does not define. Where storm damage is layered on pre-existing deterioration, what portion is excluded is exactly what the words leave open.

This excludes failure or breakdown of machinery, but COVERAGES E. 1. (c040) provides that exclusion B. 8. does not apply to losses resulting from an accident to a covered object. The two must be read together to know when machinery failure is covered.

Loss attributable to faulty "construction, workmanship or material" and to faulty "design, plan or specification" is excluded, subject to "if a covered loss ensues," with no test for separating the defect from the ensuing damage. Whether damage to the defective work itself, or to other property, is excluded is left to construction.

The exclusion of "acts or decisions, including the failure to act or decide, of any governmental employee, agent, group, organization, agency or body" overlaps GROUP A exclusion 7. (c107) on government seizure and destruction, which has its own narrower carve-back. Which exclusion governs a government-ordered loss is unresolved between them.

The list excludes "Water, land ... lawns, growing crops, or standing timber" while EXTENSIONS A. 14. (c076) grants $100,000 for loss to plants, trees and shrubs. The property-not-covered list and that extension state opposite results for the same property.

The general rule that loss "will be valued ... at replacement cost" is qualified by A. 2. (c128), which withholds replacement cost until repair or replacement actually occurs and drops to actual cash value after two years. The default and the condition state different measures of recovery for the same loss.

"We will not pay replacement cost until the lost or damaged property is actually repaired or replaced," with an actual-cash-value fallback if repairs are not made "within two (2) years after the date of the physical loss," gives no rule for a case where the insurer disputes the loss and the two years run during the dispute. What "actually repaired or replaced" requires, and when the clock starts, are both open on these words.

The alternative recovery requires that capital expenditures "were not planned as of the date of loss" and be claimed within two years, neither of which is defined or evidenced by any stated standard. Whether a given expenditure was "planned" is left to argument.

The actual cash value list is preceded by broken page and copyright text and begins at subparagraph "a." without a numbered lead-in, leaving its relationship to A. Replacement Cost unclear. The mechanical break obscures which property is valued at actual cash value.

This makes appraisal available on either party's unilateral demand, but the KANSAS CHANGES endorsement (c375) replaces it with a provision under which "an appraisal will be made only if both parties agree, voluntarily," and changes the appraiser-notice period from thirty to sixty days. Whether appraisal can be compelled turns on which text governs.

Item 2. on umpire selection is left in place by the KANSAS CHANGES endorsement, which replaces only items 1. and 3. (c375, c376), so a mandatory umpire mechanism survives inside a now-voluntary appraisal. The two must be read together to know what procedure applies in Kansas.

This makes the appraisers' written agreement binding as "the amount of our payment," while the KANSAS CHANGES replacement (c376) states the same rule followed by a truncated further sentence about an appraisal award. Whether an award binds the parties in Kansas cannot be settled from this provision alone.

"Your assignment of this policy will not be valid except with our written consent" does not distinguish assignment of the policy from assignment of an accrued claim after loss. Whether a post-loss assignment of proceeds is caught is a standard construction dispute.

This preserves coverage at unbreached locations, while CONDITIONS I. (c156) makes "this entire policy" void for fraud or misrepresentation. Whether a breach amounting to fraud voids everything or only affects the location involved is a conflict between the two conditions.

The sixty-day new-policy window stated here is replaced by a ninety-day window in the KANSAS CHANGES — CANCELLATION endorsement (c381). Both texts remain in the delivered policy stating different periods.

The list of permissible cancellation grounds here is deleted and replaced by a different list in the KANSAS CHANGES — CANCELLATION endorsement (c382), including different notice periods for the same grounds. The two lists cannot both govern a Kansas cancellation.

"The terms of this insurance will not be waived, changed, or modified except by written endorsement" purports to bar any waiver, including one arising from the insurer's own claim conduct. Whether it defeats waiver or estoppel arguments is a question this wording invites.

Reducing payment "to the extent you have collected that loss from others" overlaps CONDITIONS Q. Other Insurance (c173) and X. Subrogation (c189), which allocate third-party and other-insurance recoveries differently. Which reduction applies to a recovery from a third party is unclear across the three.

This voids "this entire policy" for fraud or misrepresentation, while the KANSAS CHANGES endorsement (c377) replaces Item I. with a provision that merely denies payment for the loss caused by the fraudulent act and requires restitution. The consequences of insured fraud differ sharply between the two.

The clause applies where a filing "would broaden this insurance without requiring any additional premium," without saying who determines that or how a partly premium-bearing filing is treated. Whether a given filing "broadens" the policy is left undefined.

The condition operates by reference to a loss payee "shown on the SCHEDULE OF MORTGAGE HOLDERS OR LOSS PAYEES, Form RM1102," a form that does not appear on the POLICY INDEX (Form RM0003) or in this policy. The condition's trigger cannot be located within the instrument.

Mortgage-holder payment depends on the schedule in Form RM1102, which is not among the forms listed on the POLICY INDEX or attached here. Who qualifies as a scheduled mortgage holder cannot be determined from the policy as issued.

"No person or organization, having custody of your covered property, will benefit from this policy" sits against the grants for personal property of others and installation property (c030, c072), which insure property held by or for others. How far the bailee bar cuts into those grants is left to construction.

This preserves limits after payment "except for those coverages written with an annual aggregate limit of liability or sublimits of liability," language that could be read to except every sublimited coverage in the policy. The scope of the exception may swallow the rule.

This makes the policy pure excess over "any other insurance that would apply in the absence of this policy," while Q. 2. (c174) contemplates proportionate contribution and Q. 3.-4. permit other insurance without reduction. The clauses state different results for the same overlap.

Proportionate contribution here is difficult to square with Q. 1. (c173), which makes this policy payable "only after the limits of all other applicable insurance are exhausted." Whether the insurer contributes or sits excess must be resolved between the two.

The insurer may elect to repair, rebuild or replace "within a reasonable period of time" and must notify "within sixty (60) days of our receipt of your proof of loss," without stating the consequence of failing to elect or to notify. What follows from an untimely or absent election is not addressed.

"When covered property consists of several parts, we will pay only for the lost or damaged part" gives no rule for matching or continuity where undamaged parts cannot be matched to replacements. Against the pair-or-set provision immediately above it, the boundary between a "part" and a "set" is undefined.

The three payment conditions are joined by "or" after item 2 while item 1 is stated as an independent requirement, so it is unclear whether compliance plus one of the other two, or any one alone, triggers the thirty-day duty. The conjunctions make the trigger genuinely ambiguous.

Coverage is limited to loss "as the result of a peril insured against during the policy period," leaving unclear whether the peril, the physical damage or the manifestation of damage must fall inside the period. In a claim for progressive or later-discovered damage that ambiguity is decisive.

"Covered losses will be adjusted with you" is qualified only by Condition M., but the ADDITIONAL NAMED INSURED endorsement (c260) separately provides that the insurer will adjust "only with you" and pay jointly with scheduled entities. Who the insurer must adjust and pay with is set out inconsistently across the two.

The recovery-sharing formula — "in the proportion that your deductible and any provable uninsured loss bears to the total loss less your proportion of fees and expenses" — is grammatically incomplete as a calculation, since the proportion is stated without the amount to which it applies. The division of a recovery cannot be computed from these words.

This imposes a two-year suit limitation while the KANSAS CHANGES endorsement (c379) deletes Item Y. and substitutes five years from the date the physical damage occurred. Which period bars a Kansas suit is a direct conflict between the two texts as delivered.

"Within two (2) years ... or the shortest time permitted by law, whichever is greater" is self-contradictory: it selects the greater of a fixed period and the shortest legally permitted period. The formula does not yield a determinate deadline.

The required protective safeguards "include, but are not limited to" the five listed items, so the insured cannot know what else must be maintained on pain of losing coverage. The open-ended catch-all against a specific list is the defect.

Subparagraph b. requiring vacant property to be valued at the smaller of actual cash value, repair cost or selling price is printed without its letter and runs on from the list in a., obscuring whether the valuation rule is a separate consequence. It also conflicts with the replacement cost basis in VALUATIONS A. 1. (c127).

"Real property is considered vacant unless at least thirty (30) percent of the square footage is" in customary use does not say whether the test is applied building by building or across a location or the policy as a whole. On a multi-building schedule that choice determines the answer.

"Give us immediate written notice of the loss" fixes no period and, unlike the Proof of Loss item, no outer date, so timeliness is measured against an undefined word. Whether notice months after a storm is "immediate" is exactly what the term leaves open.
"As soon as possible" sets no measurable deadline for the description of the loss. Compliance can only be judged by an undefined standard.

"All reasonable steps to protect the covered property from further damage" gives no benchmark for what steps are required or who bears their cost. The extent of the duty is left to argument after the fact.

A "complete inventory of the lost, damaged and destroyed property" is required without any materiality qualifier or stated consequence for an imperfect inventory. Whether an incomplete inventory forfeits the claim is left open.

The duty applies "as often as may reasonably be required," and the item is printed with orphan subparagraph letters detaching a. and b. from their text. Both the frequency standard and the list structure are indeterminate.

The examination-under-oath duty extends to "any of your agents, employees, or representatives involved in the purchase of this insurance or the preparation of your claim," a class the insured may not control, yet non-compliance is a breach of the policy. Whom the insured must produce is left uncertain.

The ninety-day sworn Proof of Loss requirement runs "from the date of loss," which in a storm claim may precede discovery, and no consequence of late submission is stated. Whether the requirement is a condition precedent to payment is not said in the text.

"A sudden, fortuitous event" is set against exclusions for "any other gradually developing condition" and for conditions correctable by maintenance, leaving no line between a sudden accident and a gradual failure that finally manifests. "Sudden" carries both a temporal and an unexpectedness sense.

"Replacement cost less deduction for depreciation" does not say what may be depreciated — materials only, or labor and overhead as well — a point that decides the size of every actual cash value payment. The formula is stated without any method.

Average daily value is computed on "the number of operating days in that period," a term the policy nowhere defines, and is applied to "the entire covered location whether or not the loss effects the entire covered location." The multiplier for a partial-location loss is therefore contestable.

Business income is "gross earnings ... less all charges and expenses which do not necessarily continue," with no test for necessity of continuation, and the PAYROLL EXPENSE endorsement (c310, c311) separately limits payroll to ninety business days. What continuing expenses are included is left open between them.

"Those locations shown on the Schedule of the DECLARATIONS" is circular here, because the Schedule (c028) shows no locations and instead says "All covered locations as per Statement of Values on file with us." The definition therefore does not identify any location by itself.

The definition can also not be squared with the DECLARATIONS Schedule note that "Insurance does not apply at locations ... unless a specific value is provided by you" (c028), which makes coverage depend on the insured's reporting rather than on what the Schedule shows. Which document fixes covered locations is the question.

"Covered loss" is confined to loss "at a covered location," although the Insuring Agreement (c009) and COVERAGES A. and B. (c029, c030) extend to property within 1,000 feet of, or in transit away from, a covered location. The definition and those grants describe different geographic reach.

"Covered property means property insured by this policy" defines the term by the conclusion it is used to reach, so it supplies no independent content. Every coverage grant that turns on "covered property" inherits that circularity.

"Other equipment capable of receiving, processing, storing or retrieving information" is a catch-all after a list of computer hardware, wide enough to capture ordinary machinery with embedded controls. What falls within the class is exactly the general-versus-specific question.

"Earth movement ... includes but is not limited to" four listed events, so the excluded class is open-ended, and it is not said whether man-made settling or soil shifting under a structure counts. The catch-all against the enumerated causes is the defect.

Extra expense is limited to costs to continue the business "as nearly normal as practicable," with "normal" defined only by reference to the condition that would have existed had no loss happened. The standard gives no way to measure which extra costs qualify.

"Property of rarity, antiquity, or artistic merit, including but not limited to" a long list makes the class open-ended and the qualifying criteria subjective. Whether an item is of sufficient "artistic merit" is undefined.

"Flood" is defined to include "surface water, rain accumulation or runoff" and spray, wording broad enough to capture ordinary rainwater entering a damaged roof. Where wind or hail opens a building and rain follows, the definition's reach against the coverage grant is contestable.

Hail is defined as stones "ranging in size from pea to softball or larger," which sets a lower bound excluding smaller hail and is stated in imprecise comparative terms. Whether a storm produced qualifying "hail" turns on a size test the policy states only by analogy.

"Miscellaneous location" is defined only as a location that is not a covered, new or unscheduled location and not one "for which coverage is found, in whole or in part, elsewhere in this policy," so its content depends entirely on the contested definitions of the other categories. Any location could be argued into or out of the class.

"Machinery and equipment principally used by you or your employees away from a covered location" turns on "principally," with no measure of how much off-premises use is required. Whether an item is mobile equipment or ordinary personal property changes both the limit and the valuation basis.

"Any storm or weather disturbance that is named by the U.S. National Weather Service" identifies a naming authority that does not itself name storms, so the trigger for the wind deductible may have no referent. Whether an unnamed severe thunderstorm or hailstorm is a "Named Storm" is left unresolved.

"Equipment ... that generates, transmits or utilizes energy" is extremely broad while the exclusions strip out structure, foundations, ductwork and piping, leaving the boundary of an "object" unclear for building systems. The subparagraph letters of the exclusion list are also missing in the delivered text.

"All loss or damage attributable directly or indirectly to one (1) cause or series of similar causes" aggregated "irrespective of the amount of time or area over which such loss or damage occurs" gives no limit on how far apart in time separate storms can be and still be one occurrence. The number of occurrences, and so of deductibles and limits, turns on that undefined phrase.

"Perils insured against means causes of loss for which this policy provides coverage" defines the term by the very question it is used to answer, giving the phrase no independent content. Every grant conditioned on a "peril insured against" inherits that circularity.

The period ends when the property "using reasonable speed" could be repaired and "made ready for operations," a hypothetical measure with no benchmark, and the numbered subparagraphs are broken across the page in the delivered text. When the period ends is left to be argued from an undefined standard.

"Any covered property subject to deterioration or impairment as a result of a change in conditions including but not limited to temperature, humidity or pressure" is broad enough to cover most stock. The open-ended "change in conditions" has no limiting principle.

The three-part definition is printed without its numbering for the first two items and with a block of page and heading text inserted mid-definition, so the list cannot be read as drafted. The class of "personal property of others" is obscured by that mechanical defect.

"Policy period means the time during which insurance is provided by this policy" is circular and does not tie to the dates in the DECLARATIONS (c007). The definition supplies no independent boundary for the many provisions that turn on the policy period.

"Any solid, liquid, gaseous or thermal irritant or contaminant, including, but not limited to" a long list, with an express exception only for ammonia, is broad enough to reach ordinary building materials and debris. The reach of the pollution exclusion depends entirely on that undefined breadth.

"Buildings and any other structure" including "permanent fittings or fixtures" and "yard fixtures" does not say where real property ends and personal property or excluded items such as pavement and land begin. For roof, pavement and outdoor items the classification decides which limit and exclusion apply.

Replacement cost here "excludes any increased cost of repair or reconstruction by reason of any law or ordinance," while EXTENSIONS B. 6. (c095) grants exactly those increased construction and building-law costs when a sublimit is shown. The definition and that extension state opposite results.

"Specified perils" includes "wind or hail," both separately defined (c256, c226) in terms — air movement "at any velocity" and stones from "pea to softball" — that do not fit the narrower notion of a specified peril. Which meaning applies where an extension turns on a specified peril must be worked out across the definitions.

Unscheduled locations are those "reported to us, but not shown on the Schedule of the DECLARATIONS," yet the Schedule shows no individual locations at all and insures by reference to a Statement of Values (c028). On that reading every reported location could be an unscheduled location, for which the Declarations show "$No Coverage".

"Wind means the direct action of the movement of air at any velocity" has no lower bound, so any air movement associated with a loss is wind. That definition drives the Named Storm deductible and the specified-perils list without any limiting content.

"You and your(s) mean the named insured shown on the DECLARATIONS," which names only Great Plains Ventures Inc, while the ADDITIONAL NAMED INSURED endorsement (c259, c263) adds eight other entities as named insureds. Whose property is "your real property," and who may sue and must perform the conditions, turns on reconciling the two.

This provides insurance to each scheduled additional named insured although DEFINITIONS V.V. (c257) confines "you" and "your" to the named insured shown on the Declarations. Whether the scheduled entities' property is "your" property for purposes of the coverage grants is left unresolved between the two.

"We will adjust any covered loss only with you" narrows the adjustment right while CONDITIONS W. (c186, c187) permits adjustment with owners of property of others and CONDITIONS L. requires joint adjustment considerations with a loss payee. Who may adjust a loss involving another entity's property is stated differently in the two places.

Payment must be made "jointly to you and any person or organization shown on the Schedule," which cuts against the same endorsement's rule that loss is adjusted only with the named insured (c260) and against CONDITIONS W. 2. Who is entitled to receive proceeds is not settled by these provisions read together.

The Schedule gives the additional named insureds' location as "Per statement of values on file with us," and lists entities (for example 3526 North Oliver, LP) whose addresses do not appear in the DECLARATIONS list of locations (c028). Whether property of a scheduled entity at an unlisted address is insured cannot be answered from the policy itself.

The limits are stacked as "we will not pay more than: A ... B ... or C," joined by "or," so it is unclear whether the schedule limit and the per-item caps apply cumulatively or as alternatives. The $1,000,000 occurrence cap that follows repeats the schedule figure without resolving that.

Reporting is due "at the time you report the values at risk, or at expiration or cancellation of this policy, whichever occurs first," with no stated consequence of failing to report. Whether the coverage is lost or merely repriced is not addressed.

The replacement cost box is left unmarked while the Schedule states a $1,000,000 limit, so mobile equipment appears to fall to actual cash value under VALUATIONS B. (c131) despite the policy's general replacement cost basis (c013). Which valuation applies to this endorsement's coverage is unresolved.

This buys back only "sudden earth movement," while GROUP A exclusion 2. (c102) excludes earth movement "whether sudden or gradual." Which losses fall in the restored band depends on a sudden/gradual line neither provision draws.

The seventy-two hour aggregation rule here differs from DEFINITIONS Z. Occurrence (c235), which aggregates all loss from one cause or series of similar causes without any time limit. Which occurrence rule governs an earth movement sequence must be resolved between the two.

The limit is "the lesser of the applicable limit of liability shown on" four different documents, without saying what to do when one of them shows no figure for the loss in question. The comparison is indeterminate where a document is silent.

The percentage machinery depends on "the deductible factor shown on the Schedule of this endorsement," but that Schedule states only flat $50,000 deductibles and no factors. The mechanism has no input to operate on.

The list of coverages excluded from earth movement cover includes Form RM1112, a form not listed on the POLICY INDEX or attached to this policy. The exclusion refers to something not part of the instrument.

The lettering of the excluded areas is corrupted ("Af = op aw >") and item H. offers "Any other location(s) shown below: Not Applicable," so the enumeration cannot be read as drafted. Which locations are excluded is obscured by the mechanical defect.

This grants flood coverage at scheduled locations although GROUP A exclusion 3. (c103) excludes flood generally, and the flood Schedule (c294) is printed with its location groups detached from the corresponding limits. Which locations enjoy the buy-back is not clear from the two read together.
The seventy-two hour flood aggregation conflicts with the open-ended aggregation in DEFINITIONS Z. Occurrence (c235). Which controls the count of flood occurrences is unresolved.

The percentage deductible mechanism operates on a "deductible factor shown on the Schedule of this endorsement," but that Schedule (c294) shows only flat dollar deductibles. The provision has no factor to apply.

The list of coverages for which no flood cover is provided includes Form RM1112, which is not among the forms listed on the POLICY INDEX or attached. The carve-out refers to a document outside the instrument.

The Schedule's location groups, per-occurrence limits, annual limits and deductibles are printed in detached columns, so it cannot be determined which of the $10,000,000, $5,000,000 and $1,000,000 limits, or which of the $50,000 and $100,000 deductibles, attaches to which Powder Tech location. The table is unreadable as drafted.

This insures loss from off-premises service interruption although GROUP A exclusion 9. (c109) excludes utility interference "if the failure occurs away from the covered location." The endorsement and the exclusion address the same event with opposite results.

The deductible is "as specified in G. 3. a. and G. 3. b. on the DECLARATIONS, Form RM1000, or on the ADDITIONAL DEDUCTIBLES AND WAITING PERIODS, Form RM1115," but those Declarations items read "$Not Applicable" (c022, c023). The cross-reference points to blanks, leaving the applicable deductible to be found elsewhere.
The time deductible is "a time period of Not Applicable immediately following the loss," which is not a period at all. Whether that means no time deductible or an inoperable condition is left open.

This makes asterisked deductibles cumulative, while DECLARATIONS G. (c027) and Form RM1115 B. (c315) say no more than the largest applicable deductible will be used. Whether deductibles stack in a service-interruption loss requires reconciling these.

The Schedule covers "All covered locations except as indicated in B., C., and D. below," but items B., C. and D. are left blank, so the exception refers to nothing. The $250,000 figure is also printed without identifying whether it is a limit or a deductible.

Payroll is paid "up to the number of business days shown on the Schedule," but "business days" is undefined and the business income definition (c213) already turns on whether charges "necessarily continue." How the ninety-day payroll cap interacts with that definition is unresolved.

The definition excepts officers, executives, managers and contract employees, then continues "and Payroll expense includes" a list of the very components just excepted, so the sentence contradicts itself grammatically. What payroll is covered cannot be read off the clause.

The endorsement's deductibles apply only "If G. 2. or G. 3. d. on Form RM1000 is marked with an (X)," but the Declarations items bearing those marks are printed with their captions detached from their amounts (c021, c023). Whether the condition to this endorsement's operation is satisfied cannot be verified within the instrument.

The largest-deductible rule is qualified by paragraph C. (c316), which makes asterisked amounts separate and additive, and by the Named Storm provision (c317), which builds a single deductible by adding factors. Whether deductibles combine in a given loss depends on these against each other.

The Named Storm deductible is built by "adding up" percentage and flat factors "listed in Paragraph C.," but paragraph C. (c319) lists factors only for first and second tier wind counties, none of which is in Kansas. Whether any Named Storm deductible applies to these Wichita locations is left unanswered.

The only deductible categories are first and second tier wind Counties and Parishes, defined in DEFINITIONS N. and L.L. (c223, c247) to include no Kansas county, so the table supplies no factor for any insured location. The tie-breaker for a location falling in "two or more of the following categories" is likewise inoperable.

The press deductibles are graded by tonnage bands whose boundaries are stated only as "250 to 1,000 tons", "1,001 to 3,000" and so on, with no rule for presses below 250 tons. Equipment outside the bands has no stated deductible.

The waiting period is stated as "Not Applicable hours," so the condition on which loss of business income and perishable goods coverage depends has no number. Whether that means no waiting period or an unsatisfiable one is left open.

The item is unmarked yet states the sublimit "is increased from $25,000 to $Not Applicable," so it is unclear whether the arson reward remains $25,000 or is eliminated. The same construction is repeated throughout this endorsement.
The unmarked item states an increase "from $25,000 to $Not Applicable," leaving unclear whether the computer virus sublimit stands or is removed. The box and the text point in different directions.

The unmarked item states an increase "from $25,000 to $Not Applicable" for deferred payments, so whether the original sublimit survives is uncertain. The form gives no rule for unmarked amendments carrying text.

The item's marking box is corrupted and it states the fine arts sublimit "is increased from $100,000 to $Not Applicable," leaving the operative sublimit uncertain. Whether the amendment took effect cannot be told from the text.

The item states the fungus cleanup sublimit "is increased from $250,000 to $Not Applicable" with its selection box corrupted, so whether the $250,000 in EXTENSIONS A. 10. b. survives is unclear. The text and the marking cannot both be given effect.

The installation sublimit is said to be "increased from $250,000 to $Not Applicable" with a corrupted selection box, so the operative sublimit is indeterminate. The provision states a change without a figure.
The lock and key sublimit is said to be "increased from $25,000 to $Not Applicable" and the selection box is missing entirely from the text. Whether any amendment applies cannot be determined.
The plants, trees or shrubs sublimit is said to be "increased from $100,000 to $Not Applicable" with no legible selection box. The clause states an amendment whose amount is not a figure.

This deletes the ninety-day temporary-location period in EXTENSIONS A. 17. b. (1) (c083) and replaces it with "up to NA days," leaving no ascertainable period of coverage at a place of safekeeping. Whether removal coverage at the temporary location survives at all is the question.

This grants up to $100,000 for contract penalties although COVERAGES C. 8. b. (2) and D. 3. e. (2) (c035, c038) exclude "fines or damage for breach of contract for late or non-completion of orders, or for penalties of any nature." The endorsement states it modifies only C. 8. b. (2), leaving the parallel extra expense exclusion untouched.

Payment requires that the insured "be found to be legally liable" under a written contract, without saying by whom — a court, an arbitrator or the insurer — or whether a negotiated payment qualifies. The trigger is undefined while paragraph 3. denies any defense obligation.

The definition says the TRIA criteria "include the following" two items, an open-ended formulation that does not state the full test for a certified act. What else must be satisfied is left outside the policy.

This adds a terrorism exclusion as item 12 of GROUP A although the DECLARATIONS record the terrorism premium as "$Declined," so the relationship between the declination and the exclusion is stated in two places without being reconciled. Whether any terrorism coverage exists must be read across both.

The fire exception gives the full limit for property "in any and all States listed on the Schedule of this endorsement" and $1,000,000 elsewhere, and Kansas is not on the schedule. The result for these Kansas locations follows only from reading the exception against the state list.

The cap is measured over "a program year (January 1 through December 31)" while the TRIA disclosure form (c387) states the same cap by reference to a "calendar year." The two descriptions of the measuring period are not identical.

The insurer pays "the reasonable extra costs of temporary repair to property or of expediting the permanent repair or replacement of the property, whichever is less," so the insured cannot choose the more effective measure. Which costs are compared, and against what baseline, is not stated.

Payment otherwise "will be determined in accordance with the valuations endorsement," but the policy contains a VALUATIONS form (RM1005) and no valuations endorsement. The cross-reference points to a document not in the instrument.

"As used here, covered property does not include animals" narrows a policy-wide defined term for this coverage only, while PROPERTY NOT COVERED (c126) already excludes animals generally. The provision either duplicates or, by implication, qualifies that exclusion.

This pays up to $100,000 to "research, replace and restore lost data," while VALUATIONS C. 4. (c135) allows only the cost of transferring from backup and expressly refuses to pay research costs. The two state opposite rules for the same expense.

Water damage resulting from an accident to an object is covered here, while GROUP A exclusion 3. (c103) excludes flood, which is defined to include surface water and rain accumulation. Which governs water escaping from equipment during a storm requires reading the two together.

"Any substance that is hazardous to health or has been declared to be hazardous to health by a governmental agency" states no threshold of hazard and no identified agency. Almost any contaminant could satisfy the first limb.

This deletes and replaces COVERAGES D. 2. (c037), substituting thirty days and a $1,000,000 limit for the twenty-one days printed in the form. Both texts are delivered, and which applies to a civil-authority extra expense claim depends on giving the endorsement effect.

This deletes and replaces COVERAGES C. 3. (c031), substituting thirty days and a $1,000,000 limit for the twenty-one days in the printed form. The delivered policy contains both provisions on the same subject.

This deletes and replaces COVERAGES C. 4. (c031), substituting thirty days and a $1,000,000 limit for the twenty-one days in the printed form. Which text governs an ingress/egress business income claim depends on the endorsement's effect.

This adds an extra expense ingress/egress extension, a coverage COVERAGES D. (c037) never granted, so it operates as a new grant rather than a replacement while the parallel business income provision was amended by deletion. Whether the extra expense exclusions in D. 3. apply to this new grant is left unaddressed.

The endorsement "applies only to covered property located in Kansas," so its appraisal, fraud and suit changes govern some property and not others under a single policy with a nationwide territory clause (c182). How the conditions operate on a claim spanning states is not addressed.

This makes appraisal available only "if both parties agree, voluntarily," replacing the unilateral demand right in CONDITIONS B. 1. (c139) and changing the notice period from thirty to sixty days. Both texts remain in the delivered policy, and whether appraisal can be compelled turns on which applies.

The final sentence is truncated — "An appraisa p i" — so the provision's statement about the effect of an appraisal award is missing. Whether an award binds the parties cannot be determined from the words delivered.

This denies only "any loss or damage caused by or resulting from" a fraudulent insurance act and requires restitution, whereas CONDITIONS I. (c156) voids the entire policy for fraud. The consequence of insured misrepresentation is stated two different ways in the same instrument.

A fraudulent insurance act requires "written statements where the known intent is to defraud," a formulation that excludes oral misstatements and leaves "known intent" undefined. Whose knowledge and what proof suffices is not stated.

This replaces CONDITIONS Y. (c190) with a five-year limitation running from "the date on which the physical damage occurred," while the form it replaces prescribes two years. Both texts are in the delivered policy and only one can bar a suit.
This substitutes a ninety-day new-policy window for the sixty-day window in CONDITIONS F. 2. (c147). The two provisions state different periods for the same cancellation right.

This substitutes a different list of cancellation grounds and notice periods for CONDITIONS F. 3. (c148), including sixty days for grounds the form allowed on ten days' notice. Which list governs a Kansas cancellation is settled only by giving the endorsement effect.

The disclosure says the terrorism premium "is shown on the DECLARATIONS" if purchased, while the Declarations show that premium as "$Declined" and the EXCLUSION OF CERTIFIED ACT(S) OF TERRORISM endorsement excludes the peril. Whether any terrorism coverage was purchased has to be read across the three.

This states the $100 billion cap by reference to a "calendar year" while the terrorism exclusion endorsement (c353) states it by reference to "a program year (January 1 through December 31)." The two descriptions of the same statutory cap are not stated identically.
